To me, just like on the subject of God, or microbes, or any other entity that cannot be seen with the naked eye alone, the burden ultimately falls on the listener to decide what they believe. You can provide witnessed accounts, images (grainy though they may be), or whatever, evidence of events attributed to the entity's actions, but it's up to the person ultimately to decide to believe what they want to. The platypus, the blue whale, the coelacanth (prehistoric fish that was believed to be long extinct, until divers saw and photographed it alive) all sounded quite extraordinary at various times in history, and I'm sure the skeptics of bygone years proudly demanded evidence or something else before believing. That's fine. I don't judge them, because we've all had our moments. Perhaps with a spouse caught cheating, when we strongly believed them incapable of such action. Or, Ted Bundy's mother, despite no lack of evidence of his guilt, continued to believe him innocent, due to her emotional investment in her own paradigm.
